title: Planes, trains and automobiles: The best ways to beat travel fatigue—so you can come home feeling rested and fulfilled
description: Five-hour flights. Eleven-hour road trips. Fifteen-hour train rides. All potentially exhausting options for the annual tradition of convening around t
body: Five-hour flights. Eleven-hour road trips. Fifteen-hour train rides. All potentially exhausting options for the annual tradition of convening around the dinner table with loved ones on Thanksgiving.An estimated 81.5 million Americans are projected to travel, or have already traveled, at least 50 miles from their homes between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, according to the American Automobile Association. And their mode of transportation is shifting: Fewer people are flying or driving this year compared to 2025, and more are traveling by buses, trains and cruises, AAA data shows.High gas prices and soaring plane ticket costs may factor into the shift. As of Wednesday evening, fuel prices are roughly 17% higher than they were on the same date in 2025, according to AAA data. Meanwhile, "months of elevated jet fuel costs due to the conflict in Iran have contributed to Thanksgiving and Christmas airfares reaching 10-year highs," according to fare-tracking platform Hopper.The alternate modes of transit may open travelers up to new experiences — and new forms of travel fatigue to keep you from returning home feeling rested and fulfilled. You're probably already familiar with the exhaustion you might get from a day of plane travel, for example. In airplanes, "there can be lower humidity, maybe lower oxygen levels at cabin pressure. Sometimes people report feeling more dehydrated or drained. You're adjusting to that change in altitude," says Alaina Tiani, a Cleveland Clinic behavioral sleep medicine psychologist. But even waiting in places like train stations or cruise ports can feel draining due to sheer sensory overload, Tiani says. And then, depending on your mode of travel, you may still need to deal with cramped seating and limited ability to get up and walk around or drink some water and eat a snack.Once you arrive at your destination, managing responsibilities like remembering where you put your hotel key and deciding what to eat and how to structure your day can also take a mental toll, says travel writer Shannon O'Donnell, who's written about managing travel fatigue. "All of that actually requires a lot more thinking and planning for your brain," she says, adding: "People just don't understand how those add up and why a relaxing vacation suddenly has them feeling wrecked."The consequences can sneak up on you, O'Donnell notes. Travel fatigue can "present as maybe a lack of interest in something that you might usually find fascinating," she says. Instead of looking out the window on a plane ride or playing car games with your kids on a road trip, you might disengage and appear apathetic to the people around you.Use these tips to manage fatigue, from a travel expert and a sleep specialistYou might stand a better chance of a fulfilling, restful holiday if you prepare for your travel fatigue. Here, Tiani and O'Donnell share their advice for how to do it:Come up with a plan before you leave to lighten the load: If you're driving, look up restaurants along your route in advance, says Tiani. Bring snacks with you to places like the airport or train station, O'Donnell suggests. Coming up with a solid itinerary for your trip can help you feel less stressed, Tiani says. She suggests scheduling a rest day in between the day you return home and when you have to get back to your everyday routine.Avoid trying to control how the trip will pan out: While planning is useful, rolling with the punches is necessary, too, O'Donnell says. "A lot of travel is being OK with things going wrong, and where you get exhausted is when you try to control more than you can," she says.Consider reasonable accommodations: Limit the number of hours you drive in a single day by adding rest stops, or pay for extra legroom on your flight if you'd benefit from it and can afford it, Tiani suggests. Prioritize sleep and downtime: Not everyone can comfortably sleep on planes, trains or buses. If you can, get some rest on the way to your destination, Tiani says. During your trip, your sleep routine likely won't be the same because you're in a different setting and operating on a new schedule, she notes.Be mindful of your diet: Stay hydrated and aim for balanced meals when you can, Tiani says. O'Donnell agrees: "For train travel and plane travel, that is one of my first sort of defenses: eating well when I get back, loading up on fresh fruits and vegetables, and refueling my body so that it can fight off anything I've been exposed to."Move your body: Walking around while traveling, including up and down the corridors of your train or plane when possible, can reduce your risk of blood clots, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Anyone traveling more than four hours by bus, car, train or plane may develop blood clots, according to the agency, though the risk is generally low for the average traveler. Exercise and sunlight exposure are especially useful for dealing with jet lag once you're back home, both Tiani and O'Donnell say.Give yourself time to decompress after your trip: After traveling, people may ask you how your travels went. Don't feel bad if you don't want to discuss the whole trip right away, O'Donnell notes. That's a form of travel fatigue itself, she says: "You will look on it differently in two weeks [or] a month's time, just let the guilt go. You don't have to feel any which way about anything. It can be an amazing trip, and also have been really hard."

schema.headline: Planes, trains and automobiles: The best ways to beat travel fatigue—so you can come home feeling rested and fulfilled

title: Taking on Starlink: Europe’s largest satellite factory opens in push to rival Musk
description: The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and r
body: The largest satellite factory in Europe was inaugurated in Belgium this week, boosting the continent's efforts to challenge Elon Musk's Starlink and reduce reliance on U.S. space infrastructure.Privately held Belgian satellite manufacturer Aerospacelab secured a 2.4-billion-euro ($2.6 billion) contract in September to manufacture 264 of the 348 satellites planned for IRIS², the European Union's answer to SpaceX's Starlink business.Aerospacelab said this will "form the backbone of Europe's sovereign, secure, and resilient connectivity infrastructure by 2030." It will be named Ectro from Nov. 30.Its new oval-shaped, 20,000-square-meter facility in southern Belgium, inaugurated by Belgian King Philippe, will be able to produce up to 500 satellites annually, which would make it the world's third-largest satellite production site, according to the Belgian royal palace. Employees are expected to move into the megafactory in January, and production is slated to begin by the end of 2028, according to AFP.CEO Aerospacelab Benoit Deper (R) guides Belgium's King Philippe - Filip of Belgium (2ndR) during a royal visit to the opening of the Aerospacelab megafactory in Marcinelle, near Charleroi on November 24, 2026. (Photo by VIRGINIE LEFOUR / Belga / AFP via Getty Images) / Belgium OUTVirginie Lefour | Afp | Getty ImagesSatellite connectivity has become increasingly important to everyday life as well as national security.It provides internet access to remote locations and defense equipment like warships and fighter jets, and lets governments and militaries communicate securely where Earth-based networks are unavailable or disrupted. The importance of such capabilities has become particularly apparent in Ukraine, as the country's military relies heavily on Starlink connectivity to fight Russian forces. Recent restrictions to the service over Russian-occupied territory reported by Ukrainian officials further underscored the way geopolitical conflict may depend on commercial businesses. But Europe still has a long way to go in challenging Starlink's dominance. SpaceX says it has more than 11,000 Starlink satellites in low Earth orbit, making it by far the largest satellite constellation in the world, and plans up to 100,000 satellites. Among the challengers is Amazon, whose satellite business, Amazon Leo, has deployed over 400 satellites and plans an initial in-orbit constellation of more than 3,200.Meanwhile, French Eutelsat operates more than 600 satellites in low Earth orbit through its OneWeb constellation. The company is also part of the SpaceRISE consortium alongside SES and Hispasat, tasked with developing and operating IRIS².The European Commission has called IRIS² a "strategic asset to achieve space sovereignty in the face of commercial satellite constellations, such as Starlink." The aim is for first launches to take place by the end of 2029, with initial services expected soon after.In August, the Commission and SpaceRISE consortium announced they were expanding the main constellation from 282 to 348 satellites, increasing its secure communications capacity for EU governments by 60%.Defense and security applications were the main drivers of the expanded scope, the Commission said.

schema.headline: Taking on Starlink: Europe’s largest satellite factory opens in push to rival Musk

title: Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher
description: US President Donald Trump speaks prior to pardoning the National Thanksgiving Turkey during a ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House in Washing
body: US President Donald Trump speaks prior to pardoning the National Thanksgiving Turkey during a ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. Aaron Schwartz | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate. That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post, suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and even multiple governorships."I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.However, the difference between the advance estimate and the figure in the second release is far from being an all-time record. It was the largest revision since the 1.2 percentage point revision seen in the second quarter of 2020.On an absolute basis, the latest revision was tied for 16th among all revisions from the advance estimate to the second release since 1990. It also tied four other quarters with a similar 0.9 percentage point difference — and was approximately double the average revision of 0.43 percentage points for all 147 quarters.The upward revision shows Trump's policies are "delivering results" that defy expectations, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC.Nothing newRevisions to U.S. economic numbers are not out of the ordinary. Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. Those data are later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.GDP data is revised repeatedly over a five year period. By the time the final revision is done, the average absolute error from the second release to the final is 1.14 percentage points.The advance estimate for Q3 U.S. GDP, which came just days before Election Day in early November, was still better than the figure economists had expected at the time. It also showed a significant step-up in growth from the second quarter.Because that was a strong showing for the economy, some on Wall Street consider this week's revision to be a confirmation of the economy's recent growth trend.Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors said immediately following the release that it "reinforces an increasingly familiar tension" that the economy is "performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes.""The economy isn't merely hanging in there. It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," the firm's chief investment officer said.Traders are currently pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December meeting, per the CME FedWatch tool. They're also anticipating an additional hike in January.— CNBC's Jeff Cox and Fred Imbert contributed reporting

schema.headline: Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher

title: Trump, NATO chief caution Russia as attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure intensify
description: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte (L) and U.S. President Donald Trump speak during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House on June 24, 2026 in
body: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte (L) and U.S. President Donald Trump speak during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House on June 24, 2026 in Washington, DC. Secretary-General Mark Rutte is meeting with the President before the annual NATO summit next month and as the Pentagon does a six-month review of American forces in Europe.Andrew Harnik | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte issued a joint statement on Thursday urging Russia not to take any actions, intentionally or otherwise, that would further expand the Ukraine war.The statement comes as Ukraine's allies sound the alarm over Russia's growing threat to European security and just one week after Trump's historic trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Asia.Trump and Rutte described their meeting at the Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida on Wednesday as "very impactful," with Russia's nearly five-year-long war in Ukraine and the Iran war among the key topics of conversation.  "We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," Trump and Rutte said in their statement.Moreover, the two discussed the importance of further increasing defense spending as well as investment in the defense industrial base in both the U.S. and NATO countries, according to the statement.Trump also said in a post on Truth Social Thursday that he "briefed NATO on the tremendous progress" being made in growing defense production, noting that the focus will be on building Patriot air defense systems, THAAD systems and Tomahawk cruise missiles, as well as "many new Weapons, both Offensive and Defensive, that have not yet been viewed by the Public, or other Countries.""There has never been a time when the United States has produced more Military Equipment or Munitions than now. Our 'cupboard' will soon be full and, when it is, our Allies and Partners throughout the World will be benefitting greatly," he said in the post.Trump's meeting with Xi and Putin, in which he described the Russian president as his "friend," sparked alarm among European lawmakers about Washington's commitment to transatlantic security.  NATO's Rutte, a seasoned diplomat known as a consensus builder during his nearly 14 years as Dutch prime minister, has repeatedly sought to de-escalate tensions in the alliance and frequently used flattery to win over the U.S. president. While some have questioned whether this approach has delivered any tangible benefits, Trump has previously described Rutte as a "great leader" and NATO's "biggest asset." Energy infrastructure attacksRussia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure in recent weeks, with further attacks on the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih overnight disrupting power supplies and bringing municipal electric public transport to a standstill, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi ​Rih's defense council.Ukrainian officials on Wednesday said Russian attacks on the country's power sector had damaged energy infrastructure and caused power outages in five regions as cold winter weather sets in. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday accused the Kremlin of "escalating" threats toward European security, citing actions in the Baltic region, Poland and on the Black Sea, and adding that "Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine." A spokesperson for Russia's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment on Thursday morning. The Kremlin has repeatedly denied seeking military confrontation with NATO countries.

schema.headline: Trump, NATO chief caution Russia as attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure intensify

title: Sovereign wealth funds are acting more like private equity giants — and inheriting their risks
description: Howard Kingsnorth | Stone | Getty ImagesFor decades, sovereign wealth funds were among private equity's most deep-pocketed backers, entrusting billion
body: Howard Kingsnorth | Stone | Getty ImagesFor decades, sovereign wealth funds were among private equity's most deep-pocketed backers, entrusting billions of dollars to buyout firms to invest on their behalf. Increasingly, they are doing the dealmaking themselves.From originating transactions and taking controlling stakes in companies to building their own investment platforms, some of the world's largest state investors are adopting the playbook of traditional private equity giants, according to industry veterans."The imminent change is that the lines between LPs and GPs are becoming increasingly blurry. This could bring more fundamental changes in the long term," Diego Lopez of Global SWF told CNBC.Limited partners, or LPs, typically commit capital to private equity funds, while general partners, or GPs, are responsible for sourcing deals and managing investments.Sovereign funds and state investment companies are increasingly taking on the GP role, Lopez said, pointing to the establishment of their own private equity management platforms, such as Mubadala Capital and Singapore's Seviora. The shift is also reflected in the way some of the world's largest sovereign investors are approaching dealmaking."They originate transactions rather than waiting for them. They build platforms rather than buying single assets. They take control positions and operate what they own," PwC said in their latest report on sovereign wealth funds. "Whether you're a company, a general partner, or a government, you'll find that these institutions are no longer the limited partner you're raising money from; they're the principal sitting across the table." Last year, Abu Dhabi's MGX, an investment vehicle established by state fund Mubadala in 2024, anchored the roughly $40 billion acquisition of Aligned Data Centers alongside BlackRock, Nvidia and Microsoft. A year earlier, a consortium led by Mubadala Capital acquired a 68% equity stake in alternative asset manager Fortress, which at the time managed more than $48 billion.Some sovereign funds are striking deals at a speed typically associated with large private equity firms, according to PwC. Singapore's GIC recorded 553 transactions between July 2023 and July 2026, Abu Dhabi's Mubadala 397 and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority 367, according to PwC's analysis of PitchBook data, which includes transactions by subsidiaries. The shift comes as sovereign wealth funds command unprecedented financial firepower. Their assets have surged about 59% over the past five years to $16.5 trillion, up from $10.4 trillion in 2022 and more than nine times the $1.8 trillion they managed in 2005, according to data provided to CNBC by research firm Global SWF which focuses on state-owned investors.PwC projects that sovereign wealth fund assets to reach $22.4 trillion by 2030.Cutting out the middlemanWhile sovereign funds' push into direct investing has been underway for years, a more challenging fundraising environment for PE firms and a resurgence in megadeals have recently accelerated the trend.The fundraising slowdown has tilted bargaining power toward large institutional investors, allowing them to negotiate more opportunities to invest directly alongside private equity managers, said Kyle Walters of PitchBook.A key attraction is the potential to save on fees. Co-investments typically carry little or no management fees and no carried interest, which is the share of investment profits that managers receive. Additionally, direct deals can eliminate external manager fees altogether."For a large SWF writing big checks, the fee savings in dollar terms can be substantial," Walters said.Sovereign funds also enjoy structural advantages over traditional buyout firms. Unlike conventional private equity funds, which operate within predetermined lifespans, sovereign investors can hold assets for decades, the experts highlighted.They can also deploy substantial sums from their own balance sheets without having to raise fresh capital, an advantage particularly valuable in capital-intensive sectors such as AI infrastructure and energy.But deep pockets and patient capital alone do not guarantee success.As sovereign wealth funds take controlling stakes in companies, they assume operational responsibilities traditionally borne by private equity managers, while potentially stretching their own capacity to source deals, conduct due diligence and manage complex assets, PwC cautioned."Building the required capability, the talent, the systems, and the governance is a slower process than committing the capital," PwC said. The firm also flagged concentration risks as sovereign investors increasingly pile into similar investment themes, particularly AI, data centers and power infrastructure, leaving even geographically diversified portfolios vulnerable to the same underlying risks.Relationship reset?Despite their growing ambitions, industry experts are skeptical that sovereign wealth funds will supplant established private equity managers."This new path these large LPs are paving is more of a partnership than a competition between GPs and LPs," Walters said, noting that much of the increased activity is taking the form of co-investments.He pointed to the $55 billion take-private deal for video-game maker Electronic Arts announced last year, in which Saudi Arabia's PIF contributed significant capital, as an example of how both sides ae joining hands.Traditional buyout firms also retain an edge in sourcing deals and managing portfolio companies."However, capital alone does not replace the specialist sourcing, operational expertise, and active ownership capabilities required to consistently create value, which experienced managers have built over time," said Vincent Ng, managing director and co-head of Asia at Partners Group.Direct investing also raises concentration risks, while illiquidity could become a problem during crises when governments need access to capital, experts said.Rather than displacing traditional buyout firms, sovereign investors' growing ambitions could change the economics of private equity, forcing managers to become more flexible in how they work with their biggest clients."This is likely to reshape the relationship between asset owners and managers, with more customized mandates, co-investments, and long-term partnerships," Ng said.

schema.headline: Sovereign wealth funds are acting more like private equity giants — and inheriting their risks

title: How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters
description: US President Donald Trump (R) prepares to shake hands with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a bilateral meeting as part of the G7 summit, i
body: US President Donald Trump (R) prepares to shake hands with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a bilateral meeting as part of the G7 summit, in Evian, eastern France, on June 17, 2026. Mandel Ngan | Afp | Getty ImagesThe latest U.S. tariff rates announced Wednesday have signaled that Washington is willing to offer India an edge over its competitors if New Delhi agrees to finalize a long-pending trade deal.The Office of the United States Trade Representative has proposed a tariff of 17% on Indian exports if New Delhi "were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade" with Washington. It added that without a trade deal, India could face tariffs of up to 25% under Section 301 investigations encompassing excess production capacity that harms U.S. interests.Meanwhile, the USTR has proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective trade deals, handing India a competitive advantage over rival exporters.The U.S. expects the announcement of a lower tariff rate will encourage New Delhi to sign off on a trade deal before the G20, Atman Trivedi, partner at Washington-based DGA Albright Stonebridge Group, told CNBC. India has got a "better bargain with Washington than its main competitors," and it may be enough for the Indian government "to declare victory and secure domestic backing for the deal," Trivedi said.In February, U.S. President Donald Trump had announced a deal with India, claiming that New Delhi had accepted to "Buy American" at a much higher level after the U.S. agreed to slash tariffs to 18% from 50% earlier. U.S. pressureThe India-U.S. trade deal has been pending with both sides indicating there was little room to grant concessions, while the Supreme Court annulling Trump tariffs allowed New Delhi to demand preferential tariffs that give it an edge over competitors."Today's announcement increases the urgency of reaching an agreement," Ronak D. Desai, visiting fellow at Hoover Institution, Stanford University, told CNBC. He added that while the prospect of a 17% tariff may strengthen the economic case for the deal, the threat of a 25% tariff could stir the sensitivity of the Indian government."The Modi government will be particularly sensitive to any perception that India is conceding under American Pressure," Desai said.India's commerce ministry on Wednesday said it "does not have structural excess capacity in any sector," denying the findings of the USTR investigation, but added that it remains committed to "working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement."Despite India facing steep tariffs, which were raised to 50%, New Delhi's trade surplus with the U.S. rose to $57.3 billion in 2025 from $45.2 billion in 2024.Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Trump are likely to meet in December for the G20 leaders' meeting in Florida, and several experts believe the two leaders could seal the trade deal on the sidelines of the summit.

schema.headline: How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters

title: China industrial profits growth surges to a 5-month high of 20.1% in October
description: Industrial robots operate on a production line manufacturing new energy vehicle parts at Jinhua Zhixin Technology Co., Ltd. on September 3, 2026 in Ji
body: Industrial robots operate on a production line manufacturing new energy vehicle parts at Jinhua Zhixin Technology Co., Ltd. on September 3, 2026 in Jinhua, Zhejiang Province of China.Vcg | Visual China Group | Getty ImagesChina's industrial profits in October grew at their fastest pace since May, building on momentum from the previous month, amid a yawning gap between tech manufacturing and consumer-facing sectors. Profits surged 20.1% in October from a year earlier, according to data released Friday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first 10 months this year, the earnings grew 16% year on year, and rose from 15.5% through September. Electronics makers drove the profit gain, with earnings in the sector doubling in the first 10 months from the same period last year, as demand for AI computing power lifted memory chips and related manufacturing, said Yu Weining, chief statistician of the NBS. Profits in high-tech manufacturing jumped 50.9%, outpacing industry as a whole, Yu added. Makers of spacecraft and launch vehicles reported a 63.2% rise.  Commodity producers also saw sharp growth in profits as demand tied to renewable energy and AI pushed up copper and aluminum prices, Yu said. Petroleum processors swung to a combined profit from a loss a year earlier.  China's economy has been running at two speeds, with AI-related manufacturing and exports powering growth while household consumption has been lagging. "The recovery has yet to broaden into a more durable improvement in corporate profitability," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, as the rebound was largely led by upstream sectors amid higher energy prices. The world's second-largest economy is estimated to have expanded 2.4% year-on-year in October, according to Capital Economics' China Activity Proxy that tracks "less politically-sensitive" activity indicators across the economy. Activity picked up "substantially" over the past couple of months, Leah Fahy, senior China economist said in a note Thursday, though the growth rate still represented a slowdown from the 3.5% pace in the first half of this year, and 3.9% in 2025.

schema.headline: China industrial profits growth surges to a 5-month high of 20.1% in October

title: Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test
description: Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data cent
body: Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials.But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects."We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth. We need every possible energy source available," Michele Della Vigna, head of natural resources research for Goldman Sachs, told CNBC. "Ultimately, what drives economic growth is energy," he added.Ben Kumar, head of strategy for wealth, investment and public policy at 7IM, suggested Latin America could benefit, given the physical materials needed for AI equipment and data centers. "We are currently neutral in the short term, but if the materials and mining cycle continues, we could see this moving to positive in a few months," he said.Where the investment case is strongestThe investment case varies across the region. Chile has copper; Argentina is expanding oil and gas exports; and Brazil has abundant renewable power and significant rare earth reserves.Chile's copper sector illustrates both the supply potential and the constraints to expanding supply. Copper production fell 8.5% in the first nine months of 2026, according to the state copper commission Cochilco, as lower ore grades, maintenance, and operational disruptions constrained supply. But demand for refined copper is set to grow 1.6% this year and 2% next year, according to the International Copper Study Group. Supply is struggling to keep pace with demand from expanding electricity grids.Chile's copper commission has raised its 2027 price forecast to $5.95 a pound, from $5.10. Codelco, the state-owned copper producer, may also have scope to increase supply, including through proposed public-private partnerships.Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, sees demand continuing to grow. "As countries expand electricity grids, they need more copper regardless of which power source they choose," he said.The scale of the opportunity will depend in part on how quickly energy demand grows. Goldman Sachs forecasts that global power demand for data centers will grow by 170% by 2030. The IEA projected in April that global data center electricity consumption would rise from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030.Turning resources into investment A mineral exploration mine near Sao Felix do Xingu, Para state, Brazil, on Monday, Oct. 4, 2021. Destruction of the Brazilian Amazon accelerated this year to levels unseen since 2006, with more than 5,019 square miles of forest lost between August 2020 and July 2021. Photographer: Jonne Roriz/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe investment case also depends on whether the region can capture more value from the resources it produces. Latin America and the Caribbean refined only 26% of the copper they mined in 2025, according to the IEA."Cautious optimism is justified and there will be massive critical mineral demand," said Monica de Bolle, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics."But improving refining capacity will be crucial to capture more of that value," she added.Some projects have already secured financing. Chilean explorer Marimaca Copper Corp selected a preferred lender for a $400 million debt facility to build a mine on Oct. 28. The funding will go towards developing an open-pit mine in the north of Chile that will produce 50,000 metric tons of refined copper annually. Production is expected from 2029.Argentina shows the other side of the opportunity: strong oil and gas resources, but insufficient infrastructure to get more production to global markets."I see an opportunity in the infrastructure that gets Argentine oil and gas to market. A producer in Vaca Muerta can have excellent wells and still struggle to expand exports without pipeline capacity and access to ports.That gives investors a reason to look at transport and export infrastructure alongside production," Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, added. Vaca Muerta is Argentina's vast shale basin.Argentina is also attracting investment in drilling and export infrastructure. International capital markets have reopened to investment in drilling and pipelines in Argentina. That investment has already driven the build-out of a pipeline and port. Argentina will then be able to export far more crude oil. Chevron and American oil tycoon Harold Hamm have also increased their investments in Argentina.Brazil's case rests partly on its renewable-heavy power mix. About 89% of the country's electricity was generated from renewable sources in 2025, according to the country's Ministry of Mines and Energy."That puts Brazil in a strong position to benefit as AI and data centers drive up demand," Stephanie Link, chief investment strategist and portfolio manager at Hightower Advisors, told CNBC.But while Brazil has the world's second-largest reported rare-earth reserves, its estimated mine production is far smaller than China's. USGS estimates put Brazil's output at 2,000 metric tons in 2025, compared with China's 270,000 metric tons. Brazil's reserves are estimated at 11 million metric tons by the USGS, second only to China's 44 million metric tons. For investors, the gap between Brazil's vast reserves and limited current production is both the opportunity and the execution risk.Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva speaks during a press conference at the Brazilian Embassy after his White House meeting with US President Donald Trump in Washington, DC on May 7, 2026. President Trump hailed talks at the White House with "very dynamic" Brazilian counterpart Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Thursday, saying his meeting with his ideological opposite focused on tariffs. (Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP via Getty Images)Saul Loeb | Afp | Getty ImagesThe risks to watchFor investors, the policy question is whether governments can make projects viable and keep them on track. Luis Costa, Citi's global head of emerging markets strategy, said governments need to offer incentives, particularly in the early stages of projects, because infrastructure lags the region's resource wealth. He also stressed that support must last: infrastructure projects can take several years to develop.The World Bank's Latin America and the Caribbean Economic Update for 2026 projects growth for the region of 2.2%, and highlights the "restricted fiscal space, sticky inflation and high borrowing costs.""The economic policy and fiscal policy needs to get in line as markets are globally becoming more sensitive to fiscal stories," said Costa.Brazil will need to establish fiscal credibility to attract investment, particularly if higher public spending puts additional pressure on debt and borrowing costs. "If investors doubt the government can stabilize public debt, companies' long-term financing costs could stay high even as the central bank lowers its policy rate," Ch added.With Argentina set for national elections in October 2027, political continuity will also matter for energy investment. "A return to tighter currency controls or persistent deficits would make companies more likely to delay projects, even in an oil field with attractive economics," said Ch.BUENOS AIRES, ARGENTINA - APRIL 2: Argentine President Javier Milei sings the national anthem during a ceremony to remember the 44th anniversary of the Malvinas war at Plaza San Martin on April 2, 2026 in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Argentina honours the 649 soldiers killed in action as well as the war veterans. (Photo by Tomas Cuesta/Getty Images)Tomas Cuesta | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesPro-business President Javier Milei faces a tight race for re-election, though a change in leadership would not necessarily undermine medium- to long-term investment."There is also the possibility of a pragmatic Peronist ticket emerging, which markets would be satisfied with," said Nicolas Jaquier, emerging-market fixed-income portfolio manager at Ninety One.For those governing across Latin America, policies to unlock its wealth of resources will be key for it to emerge as a winner from the AI demand boom."Supply chain security is becoming more and more relevant, and if commodities take off Latin America can be a clear and obvious winner," said Kumar.

schema.headline: Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test

title: Robots could be doing household chores in just 1-2 years, Chinese EV firm says
description: The XPeng Inc. IRON humanoid robot at the company's AI Day event in Guangzhou, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Image
body: The XPeng Inc. IRON humanoid robot at the company's AI Day event in Guangzhou, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBEIJING — The household robot could soon become a reality, Brian Gu, co-president of Xpeng, a Chinese electric car company which has entered the humanoids space, told CNBC."Maybe after successful deployment into commercial settings, maybe another one to two years, we can start thinking about deploying into home settings," Gu said. "Technology is moving at a much faster clip." Xpeng revealed its latest general-purpose humanoid robot Iron on Wednesday. The company plans to start training the robot as a store assistant in its retail car locations in the first quarter next year, after starting mass production in January. Sales are set to begin in the second quarter, with deliveries expected later in the year.Founded in 2014 as an electric car company, Xpeng beat Tesla to rolling out driver-assist in mainland China. The Chinese automaker has launched its own artificial intelligence chips. It's also expanded into personal flying vehicles and robotics. The robotics unit this summer raised $900 million at a $6.3 billion valuation in its first funding round, led by IDG Capital. Investors, however, appear to be a tad skeptical about the developments at Xpeng, with the downturn in the Chinese auto market also weighing on the company. Xpeng's shares, listed in both New York and Hong Kong, have dropped more than 55% this year amid broad sector declines.China's humanoid industry has faced more regulatory scrutiny on financing in recent months after Unitree's high-profile IPO and stock slump, as well as a rush of capital into the sector. That's all raised questions about commercialization and the efficacy of the core tech.Gu said Xpeng's robotics stands out for its rare combination of the hardware, software and real-life use cases. He's expecting to add more investors after Iron's planned commercial launch next year."You can always make the head talk, you can always make the leg run, you can always make the hands to do certain tasks," Gu said. "But doing a task while you're walking and answering questions at the same time, that's the most challenging part. And then doing everything well, not falling down, not getting distracted. The model has to work in sync."Most humanoid robot startups, especially in China, focus on a portion of the tech, such as hands or the artificial intelligence-powered brain. Some in the industry also see themselves as original equipment manufacturers, with another company tying the parts together for the finished robot.But that may be easier said than done.Xpeng's co-founder and CEO He Xiaopeng, a software engineer, always thought that software could solve "everything,'" Gu said. "And after he got into the EV business he realized how hard it is to make hardware ... really do the things that you want to do safely and consistently." On Wednesday, Xpeng announced its "Turing Physical AI Architecture" for using AI and real-time decision-making tech to control cars and humanoids.Gu told CNBC that Xpeng's robotics development only needs the driver-assist chips, which the company already has, indicating limited impact from U.S. restrictions on advanced Nvidia chip sales to China."Right now we don't see any change to our supply chain, and also ability to have these chips."In 2023, Xpeng's then-head of autonomous driving, Xinzhou Wu, left to lead Nvidia's automotive chip business.As Xpeng ramps up its humanoid robotics business, Gu said the company's existing work in autonomous driving technology translates easily to a new product line — with far higher profit margins. "It's much easier to be profitable for the robotics business than the autos business." Robotics will likely become a meaningful part of Xpeng's business in two to three years, Gu said, with profitability coming as soon as next year. That value will "dramatically" increase with robots entering households, he said. But Gu noted that compared to commercial environments, homes require robots to act safely around elderly people, children and pets, in addition to reacting to emergency situations. That increases requirements for battery power and performance consistency, he said.

schema.headline: Robots could be doing household chores in just 1-2 years, Chinese EV firm says

title: ‘Ready for any storm’: UAE minister optimistic on economy as IMF lifts forecast
description: Minister of Economy and Tourism, Abdulla Bin Touq Al Marri, speaks during a press briefing held by the UAE government following Iranian strikes, in Ab
body: Minister of Economy and Tourism, Abdulla Bin Touq Al Marri, speaks during a press briefing held by the UAE government following Iranian strikes, in Abu Dhabi on March 3, 2026. Iran stepped up its attacks on economic targets and US missions across the Middle East on March 3, as the US president warned it was "too late" for the Islamic republic to seek talks to escape the war. As drones and missiles crashed into oil facilities and US embassies in the Gulf, Washington's ally Israel bombarded targets in Iran and pushed troops deeper into Lebanon to battle the Tehran-backed militia Hezbollah. (Photo by Ryan Lim / AFP via Getty Images)Ryan Lim | Afp | Getty ImagesThe UAE is "very optimistic" about achieving 7%-8% growth next year, the country's economy and tourism minister Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri told CNBC after the latest data from the International Monetary Fund showed the country would avoid a recession in 2026.The IMF last week revised the UAE's real GDP forecast to 0.2% growth in 2026 from a 3.9% contraction predicted a month ago. "The UAE is coming back, and that adjustment within one month shows that there is a huge potential aspect when it comes towards the end of the year," the minister told CNBC's Dan Murphy.He said the tourism industry was already picking up with occupancy rates returning to "almost near normal" and international carriers including British Airways and Air France rerouting flights to the UAE. The minister expects economic growth to be higher than 0.2% this year. The Iran war has disrupted economic activity in the UAE, with missile and drone attacks from Tehran and maritime disruptions weighing on energy trade, tourism, aviation and private-sector confidence.Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump said that renewed attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" if negotiations produce a "very strong agreement." However, on Monday, Trump threatened that Tehran could face fresh U.S. strikes next year if the two countries failed to strike a deal, as per Fox News.   "We can we cannot promise the world for any storms that will land on our shore, but we can always promise that the UAE's economy is ready for any storm," Al Marri said. He added that next year the UAE's economy will have a "different" model than the one before the conflict and investments will be focused on building factories and "things that we really need in times of crisis."The World Bank in October said it expects the UAE's economy to recover next year, driven by rising oil production and exports and a rebound in tourism, trade, transportation, financial services, and construction. It warned that the improvement in economic activity in the UAE largely depends on the duration and intensity of the Iran war, with a faster de-escalation likely to accelerate the recovery in services exports and private-sector activity.

schema.headline: ‘Ready for any storm’: UAE minister optimistic on economy as IMF lifts forecast

title: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to purchase GPUs, sources say
description: Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources tol
body: Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC. It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. 16. Chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information.The interim final rule was announced by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China.Prior to the new rule's announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.The new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.Nvidia and the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Closing 'loopholes'The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.watch nowU.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes.""Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries," he said.U.S. lawmakers have been looking to clamp down on China's access to advanced compute.Separately, Nvidia warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

schema.headline: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to purchase GPUs, sources say

title: What is ‘texture-maxxing’? The food trend putting crunch on the menu
description: A man and a woman are eating food together. The woman is eating a piece of food with her mouth openAlrphoto | Moment | Getty ImagesTexture-maxxing is
body: A man and a woman are eating food together. The woman is eating a piece of food with her mouth openAlrphoto | Moment | Getty ImagesTexture-maxxing is the latest food trend taking social media by storm as consumers, driven by aesthetics and taste, look for a sensory experience. British supermarket Waitrose's latest food and drink report highlighted "texture-maxxing" as one of the trends of the year. It describes the phenomenon as a multi-sensory indulgence that is "fuelled by texture-maxxing crunch and intense flavour hits," pushing shoppers to fill their trolleys with crunchy peanut butter, dumplings, and trifles."This year, the sound of food went mainstream," Waitrose's Senior Development Chef Will Torrent said in the Wednesday report. "Driven by social media's obsession with audible, multi-sensory cooking, we're creating high-contrast meals that combine shatter-crisp crunch with pillowy chew." "The emphasis in social media content has flipped from narrative voiceovers to ASMR-inspired audio, where the evocative sounds of food are just as important as the visuals," he added.Food trends on social media have ranged from the obvious to the absurd. Fibermaxxing and proteinmaxxing have taken off in the past few years. Meanwhile, food and beverages like Dubai chocolate, protein coffee, and ube were some of the big social media hits. Nestlé's USA 2026 trends found that 75% of Gen Z and 80% of millennials sought out texture in snack cravings with the hashtag "crunchtok," amassing 1.5 billion views. Waitrose noted that shoppers looking to maximize on texture bought its viral No.1 Alphonso Mango Dessert, which involves "cracking through the crisp shell" to access a "smooth mango mousse and passion fruit curd on a crunchy white chocolate base." Waitrose's TikTok and Instagram videos of eating the dessert were watched by more than two million people, with a whopping 6,173 hours and 36 minutes of play time on TikTok. Its videos featuring crunchy toast also went viral. The U.K. grocer's sales of jarred chili crunches, which include crispy rayu oils such as itsu Crispy Chilli Oil, saw a 13-fold jump. Meanwhile, crunchy peanut butter outsold smooth. Dumplings also had a moment, with sales of chicken gyoza dumplings up 116% this year and searches on waitrose.com for gochujang and peanut butter udon noodles jumped 60%. "We've seen an explosion in demand as shoppers treat dumplings not just as a quick weeknight bite, but as a total sensory experience," Waitrose's Executive Chef Stephen Parkins-Knight said. "Driven by the rise of texture-maxxing, people want that ultimate contrast: delicate skins, juicy fillings and crispy skirts, topped with very chilli crunch. With innovation ranging from fusion fillings to rich dipping broths, dumplings have taken a delicious centre stage in 2026," he added.Texture-maxxing also extended to desserts, as shoppers bought twice as many chocolate trifles compared to 2025, and sales of strawberry trifles increased 160%.Tiramisu was also popular, with searches for waitrose.com's tiramisu recipe page increasing 155% year-on-year.

schema.headline: What is ‘texture-maxxing’? The food trend putting crunch on the menu

title: ‘Your booth is waiting’: Denny’s welcomes Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO
description: Denny's restaurant logo sign is seen in Pennsylvania, United States, on August 8, 2026. (Photo by Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nu
body: Denny's restaurant logo sign is seen in Pennsylvania, United States, on August 8, 2026. (Photo by Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesJensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia — and Denny's has a booth waiting for him.The American diner chain welcomed the billionaire's return as Nvidia CEO by revealing that it had reinstated a commemorative plaque marking the birthplace of the artificial intelligence chip giant after learning of its removal on Nov. 13."Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's said in a post on X.The plaque marks the booth at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley, California, where Huang and his co-founders discussed the idea for Nvidia, which was founded in 1993.The restaurant chain said it learned on Nov. 13, a day after Huang's resignation, that the plaque had been removed."We put the plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's said, without specifying who had removed it or why.Read more Nvidia newsHuang reinstatement reignites voter angst over tech's outsized powerJensen Huang's Nvidia return highlights U.S.-China AI talent raceNvidia whiplash tests Kevin Warsh's push to read market signals: LiesmanAI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeezeJensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession planTrump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in WashingtonAG Blanche, FBI's Patel dodge questions about Huang investigationCongress blasts Nvidia bringing Jensen Huang backJensen Huang to face Congress the same day as Nvidia GTCHuang's ties to the diner chain, however, stretch back well before Nvidia's founding. He worked at Denny's as a teenager, washing dishes and serving customers before going on to build one of the world's most valuable companies.The restaurant chain also disclosed that it had contacted Nvidia's communications team on Nov. 10 to express its pride in their shared history.Huang's return came less than two weeks after his sudden resignation rattled investors and raised questions about corporate governance and succession planning at the chipmaker.While his return has put those issues in the spotlight, Denny's offered a simpler message to its former employee."Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on. We're always open, 24/7," the restaurant chain said.

schema.headline: ‘Your booth is waiting’: Denny’s welcomes Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO

title: Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value
description: Zheka-boss | Istock | Getty ImagesAs the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand
body: Zheka-boss | Istock | Getty ImagesAs the high cost of living squeezes consumers' wallets this holiday season, more shoppers are turning to secondhand retail and thrifting.The shift comes as consumers look for better value, buyers put more emphasis on personalization and younger generations change the way they shop. The U.S. secondhand apparel market grew 13% in 2025, nearly four times faster than the overall retail clothing market, according to GlobalData.That segment is expected to reach nearly $80 billion by 2030, growing more than 7% annually on average, GlobalData found. Much of that expansion — 40% — was driven by Generation Z, followed closely by millennials."I think this has been their version of the thrill of the hunt that millennials loved during the recession days," Katherine Cullen, a global senior retail analyst at EY, told CNBC. "It's a way to really express an individual style, find something unique, something that really fits their own vibe and personality."It goes beyond people shopping for themselves, Cullen said. With more emphasis on unique holiday gifts, shoppers are leaning more on secondhand retail than they have before, whether in clothing or in other retail categories.They're looking for something that fits the personality of the person they're shopping for, she added.For Vanessa Roberts, that meant finding two antique children's chairs that she says will perfectly round out her nieces' play space. Roberts, 37, said she's been thrifting for at least two decades, each time embracing the "thrill" of finding something unique or vintage.Especially in fashion, at a time when the quality of mass-produced items has decreased, thrifted items offer more value beyond just the price tag, Roberts added."It's crazy that you can find better quality items at the thrift store right now from 20 years ago versus what you can find at stores right now," she said. Roberts, who lives in Los Angeles, said she began shopping for holiday gifts in September. As she prepares her haul for December, roughly 70% of her gifting will come from secondhand stores, she estimated."It's been a fun little challenge, where it's like a little scavenger hunt when I go into the thrift store," she said. "I'm definitely thrifting for the holidays – I do it every year."Emphasis on valueThe trend coincides with an economy that has forced consumers to be more intentional about how they spend, as they face high inflation and elevated gas prices.In October, the consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, which was more than anticipated. Still, consumers are expected to continue spending through the holiday season, with sales projected to top $1 trillion for the first time — though some of that estimated increase is boosted by inflation."You have a consumer who, while they're willing to spend at the top level, they're willing to splurge selectively," Cullen said. "Consumers are looking for value, which I think is something that is making secondhand resale and re-commerce more attractive."And while clothing is largely the entry point to buying resale, secondhand shopping is increasingly expanding into furniture, electronics and books, according to a report from consumer insights firm The Consumer Collective.Its October report found that 34% of people surveyed said secondhand products offer better value than brand new ones. Many secondhand items also have an inherent added value beyond the low price on the tag, according to eBay CEO Jamie Iannone. The uniqueness of those products, as well as the allure that vintage adds to them, means consumers may actually be seeking the benefits of secondhand in more ways than one."I can buy a product that's used, and it almost has cachet around it," Iannone told CNBC. "Consumers today, they're able to get these amazing values on products, and it's seen as very normal to be gifting pre-loved."According to eBay's Recommerce Report in October, 70% of global consumers surveyed said they consider secondhand shopping important for managing their budgets. That same report also found that 89% of respondents plan to spend the same amount or more on secondhand products next year compared with this year.Iannone said he thinks the interest in secondhand this holiday season is "much stronger" than last year."It's becoming just a more established part of consumers' shopping and gifting routines," he said. The era of personalizationFound Boston vintage market at the former SoWa Power Station, March 29, 2026.Matthew J. Lee | Boston Globe | Getty ImagesAt a time when algorithms are driving shopping trends, consumers are also looking for ways to distinguish themselves and their purchases.That's stretching beyond buying for themselves to purchasing holiday gifts for others, too."Secondhand is where they're finding unique items to wear," Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at ThredUp, told CNBC. The company's holiday survey found that respondents valued uniqueness nearly as much as the value of a thrifted piece. "To me, that represents a pretty meaningful shift in consumer taste," he added.It's partly why ThredUp, which is an online thrift marketplace, emphasizes that each of its products is "a snowflake," Rotem said — something unique.That's the appeal of buying preowned, rather than purchasing off the rack that hundreds of other people are reaching for, too. "Consumer tastes have changed, and they're much more into vintage," he added. "Uniqueness has a premium in their minds."Larger retailers are taking note, EY's Cullen said. More retailers, such as Lululemon, Patagonia and Madewell, are dabbling in preowned.Wall Street is also increasingly watching the growing secondhand trend. Though shares of some secondhand and resale companies such as eBay and Savers Value Village have climbed this year, shares of both ThredUp and The RealReal have tumbled year to date. "There's a lot of conversation around authenticity or the best find," Cullen said. "I think that interest and momentum, along with some of the economic factors that we're all facing, the idea that people are looking to be frugal is going to just continue."

schema.headline: Secondhand shopping is going mainstream this holiday season as consumers seek value

title: SpaceX, Musk pledge to donate a share each to active Trump Accounts
description: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk speaks to reporters as President Donald Trump looks on outside the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026.Tierney L. Cross | T
body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk speaks to reporters as President Donald Trump looks on outside the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026.Tierney L. Cross | The Washington Post | Getty ImagesSpaceX said Wednesday it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account, and CEO Elon Musk would personally match the gift. "SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit." The White House announced in October that nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through auto-enrollment. It's unclear how many are considered active. Musk said in a social media post on X on Thursday that the share from SpaceX would be transferred next month, without providing further details. "The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," he added.Eligible children must have their account claimed to enable contributions from family members, friends and employers, and to receive the government's one-time $1,000 seed contribution. Auto-enrolled children can receive philanthropic contributions without a parent or guardian claiming an account, according to TrumpAccounts.gov.Representatives for SpaceX and the U.S. Department of the Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for further details about the planned gift. SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell had previously agreed to make a personal gift of over 2 million SpaceX shares to Trump Accounts, with eligible account holders expected to receive them in December.In October, Elon Musk posted on X that he would give a share of SpaceX to every kid in America next year.Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027. Since the July 4 launch, families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts. Total deposits now sit at more than $9 billion, CNBC first reported. Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria. The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations, a move officials have said is meant to encourage more philanthropic gifts.Contributing stock can benefit donors, who are able to avoid capital gains taxes triggered by selling appreciated stock. But families can face restrictions related to selling that donated stock. The policy also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.Under U.S. Department of the Treasury guidelines, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17.SpaceX shares have been under some pricing pressure as the company negotiates a possible merger with Elon Musk's automaker Tesla. The companies have established two special committees to handle merger negotiations, and hired advisers for a potential mega-deal. CNBC's Sam Meredith, Kevin Breuninger, Kate Dore and Jess Dickler contributed to this story

schema.headline: SpaceX, Musk pledge to donate a share each to active Trump Accounts
